newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Dec 20.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Dec 20.

text.p: Treasurer Winston Peters has raised the prospect of another round of cost-cutting in the public service, saying he believes there is still fat in the system. Peters, who on Thursday held his first press conference as Treasurer, said coalition ministers would have to present information on savings that could be made to a February 4 Budget meeting. Slashing government spending in low priority areas is seen as one way of financing the spending promises such as free doctor visits for those under five. Peters denied that what was under way was a revival of the "razor gang" that cut spending six years ago but
said there would be a "gatekeeping operation" to ensure quality of spending. Page 1.

The Serious Fraud Office and the Inland Revenue Department are to investigate claims of improper mortgagee sales after an internal investigation at the Housing COrporation. Corporation chairman Michael Cashin said inquiries were made after an informant provided material alleging impropriety in some mortgagee sales. The allegations related to the actions of an agent for the corporation and a third party. Page 1.

National and NZ First on Thursday signed off last-minute sweeteners to add to their main coalition agreement, promising to look at further compensation for victims of bad blood and setting up a legal fund for victims of British nuclear testing on Christmas Island. National and NZ First last week made public the main coalition package, worth about $5.4 billion in extra spending over three years. However, the coalition government on Thursday issued a one-page addendum, covering "outstanding matters" that were hurriedly agreed to in the final day of the National-NZ First coalition talks. Page 2.

New Zealand's return to higher levels of economic growth may be hampered by the coalition government's deferral of tax cuts, a report published on Thursday by the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development says. The OECD's Economic Outlook for 1996 says the economy, which has been one of the strongest performing in the 28-country group during the past four years, has seen growth slow to 1.2 percent from a high of five percent in 1994. The report says the first round of tax cuts this year raised the prospect of a consumer-led recovery, but this could be jeopardised if the second round does not proceed. Treasurer Winston Peters defended the coalition government's spending programme on Thursday, saying $1.2 billion proposed for next year was not significantly different to the amount that would have been spent on the tax cuts. Those cuts have been deferred to pay for the social spending agreed to by National to secure the support of NZ First. The spending programme is under fire from Labour and from Bankers Trust chief economist David Plank, but Peters said the programme was "very prudent". Plank said a Bankers Trust analysis showed it would be "difficult, if
not impossible" for the government to fit the extra spending under the cap. Page 2.

Fletcher Energy shares jumped 11 cents to $4.02 on Thursday after news of a decision to proceed with the development of an oilfield off Brunei. Fletcher Energy owns 35 percent of the Maharaja Lela gas and condensate field, with proven reserves of 90 million barrels of oil equivalent. Development should begin next year, with production scheduled for early 1999 at a cost of NZ$30 million. Fletcher Energy chief executive Michael Andrews said on Thursday the size of the field was difficult to

determine, and the decision to go ahead was made on the basis of proven reserves alone. Andrews said the development would give the company strong cash flows, a stable presence and access to processing facilities close to Asian markets. Page 14.

Treasurer Winston Peters has left open the question of whether the Reserve Bank would be expected to target anything but price stability. At a press conference in Wellington on Thursday night, Peters was asked if the Reserve Bank would target anything but price stability. After just three days in his new job, a cautious Peters said: "You are not going to get a

response to that question today. That is a matter I would prefer to answer in the new year, after I have had time to talk to the Reserve Bank and others," he said. Businesses should hold on "a little longer" in the face of a higher dollar, till they got a clear fix on the shape, framework and character of the new coalition government, Peters said. Page 14.

Affco chairman Peter Jackson took a swipe on Thursday at politicians who "blithely made statements that the exchange rate had little effect on farmers' returns". He told shareholders at the company's annual meeting in Auckland -- many of them farmers

-- that the strong dollar was affecting them to a massive extent and that low inflation was being achieved through "screwing to death" the export sector. Jackson said the rising dollar had wiped more than $1 billion off returns to sheep and beef farmers in the past two years. Page 14.

Involvement as one of the main sponsors of the America's Cup-winning Team New Zealand had been critical in securing contracts to build boats for export to Japan, Toyota New Zealand managing director Bob Field said on Thursday. The 12-month contract could be expanded if the 15 luxury cabin cruisers
proved a success in Japan, with potential for about $40 million worth of exports by 2000, Field said. Page 14.
